etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English atteynen, from Anglo-Norman ataindre, from Old French, from Latin attingō. Doublet of attainder and attinge.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To gain (an object or desired result).

quote.citation: 1595 December 9 (first known performance), William Shakespeare, “The life and death of King Richard the Second”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies: Published According to the True Originall Copies (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene iii]:
quote.text: Lord Ross. Your presence makes us rich, most noble lord. / Lord Willoughby. And far surmounts our labour to attain it.

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 63, in Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC, page 572:
quote.text: […]  he will stick at no falsehood, or hesitate at no crime, to attain his ends.

quote.citation: 1885, W[illiam] S[chwenck] Gilbert, Arthur Sullivan, composer, chapter I, in  […]  The Mikado; or, The Town of Titipu, London: Chappel & Co., […], →OCLC, Act I, page 6:
quote.text: […]  that’s the highest rank a citizen can attain!

quote.citation: 1937, George Orwell, The Road to Wigan Pier‎[1], New York: Harcourt, Brace, published 1958, Part 1, Chapter 5, p. 82:
quote.text: [S]olitude is never easy to attain in a working-class home

quote.citation: 1964 July, S. W. Smart, “The Southern needs no centralised Control”, in Modern Railways, page 50:
quote.text: But an absolutely right time arrival of all trains on the same day is never attained.

quote.citation: 2007, Mohsin Hamid, chapter 11, in The Reluctant Fundamentalist‎[2], Orlando: Harcourt, page 157:
quote.text: Where else could I  […]  hope to attain such an impressive income?

definitions.definition: (transitive) To reach or come to, by progression or motion; to arrive at (a place, time, state, etc.).

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene v]:
quote.text: […]  my bones would rest, / That have but labour’d to attain this hour.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book X”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC, line 1026:

1791 (date written), Mary Wollstonecraft, “Observations on the State of Degradation to which Woman is Reduced by Various Causes”, in A Vindication of the Rights of Woman: With Strictures on Political and Moral Subjects, London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson, […], published 1792, →OCLC, page 150:
quote.text: It has also been asserted, by some naturalists, that men do not attain their full growth and strength till thirty; but that women arrive at maturity by twenty.

quote.citation: 1816 June – 1817 April/May (date written), [Mary Shelley], chapter III, in Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus. […], volume I, London:  […]  [Macdonald and Son] for Lackington, Hughes, Harding, Mavor, & Jones, published 1 January 1818, →OCLC:
quote.text: the southern gales  […]  blow us speedily towards those shores which I so ardently desire to attain

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To come or arrive, by motion, growth, bodily exertion, or efforts toward a place, object, state, etc.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Psalm 139:6:
quote.text: Such knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is high, I can not attain unto it.

quote.citation: 1611, The Holy Bible, […] (King James Version), London:  […]  Robert Barker, […], →OCLC, Acts 27:12:
quote.text: if by any means they might attain to Phenice

quote.citation: 1782, William Cowper, letter to Joseph Hill dated 11 November, 1782, in Private Correspondence of William Cowper, London: Henry Colburn, 1824, Volume 1, p. 222,[3]
quote.text: You may not, perhaps, live to see your trees attain to the dignity of timber—I, nevertheless, approve of your planting, and the disinterested spirit that prompts you to it.

quote.citation: 1810, Walter Scott, “Canto I. The Chase.”, in The Lady of the Lake; […], Edinburgh:  […]  [James Ballantyne and Co.] for John Ballantyne and Co.; London: Longman, Hurst, Rees, and Orme, and William Miller, →OCLC, stanza VII, page 10:
quote.text: For, scarce a spear’s length from his haunch, / Vindictive toiled the blood-hounds staunch; / Nor nearer might the dogs attain, / Nor farther might the quarry strain.

quote.citation: 1874, John Richard Green, A Short History of the English People‎[4], London: Macmillan, Chapter 2, Section 6, p. 90:
quote.text: Few boroughs had as yet attained to power such as this,

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To get at the knowledge of.

quote.citation: 1655, Thomas Fuller, “Section II”, in The Church-history of Britain; […], London:  […]  Iohn Williams […], →OCLC, (please specify |book=I to XI):
quote.text: […]  Master Camden, sometimes acknowledgeth, sometimes denieth him for an English Earle. Not that I accuse him as inconstant to himself, but suspect my self not well attaining his meaning therein.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To reach in excellence or degree.

quote.citation: 1625, Francis [Bacon], “Of Innovations”, in The Essayes […], 3rd edition, London:  […]  Iohn Haviland for Hanna Barret, →OCLC, page 139:
quote.text: Yet notwithstanding as Those that first bring Honour into their Family, are commonly more worthy, then most that succeed: So the first President (if it be good) is seldome attained by Imitation.

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To reach a person after being behind them.

quote.citation: 1622, Francis, Lord Verulam, Viscount St. Alban [i.e. Francis Bacon], The Historie of the Raigne of King Henry the Seventh, […], London:  […]  W[illiam] Stansby for Matthew Lownes, and William Barret, →OCLC, page page-174:
quote.text: The Earle finding  […]  the enemie retired, pursued with all celeritie into Scotland; hoping to haue ouer-taken the Scottish King, and to haue giuen him Battaile; But not attaining him in time, sate downe before the Castle of Aton  […]  which in a small time hee tooke.
